name: Traceability Matrix - TPP
rows: 02. Entity Protective Security Roles and Responsibilities
The Accountable Authority is responsible for managing the security risks of their entity.
Portfolio planning can create or reduce enterprise security risk; governance must align to PSPF accountability for managing those risks.
Direct - applies to all NDIA application, infrastructure and data portfolio decisions with material security risk.
NDIA technology portfolio decisions must identify security risks and escalate material residual risks through approved governance for Accountable Authority awareness or decision.
02. Entity Protective Security Roles and Responsibilities
A Chief Information Security Officer is appointed to oversee the entity's cyber security program and the cyber security for the entity's most critical technology resources.
Critical technology resources require CISO oversight so cyber risk is considered before investment, retention or rationalisation decisions.
Direct - the CISO must be engaged for cyber risk impacts across the ICT portfolio.
The CISO, or authorised delegate, must be a required stakeholder for portfolio decisions affecting critical technology resources or cyber risk posture.
Executive reporting, assurance evidence and monitoring
02. Entity Protective Security Roles and Responsibilities
The Chief Information Security Officer is accountable to the Accountable Authority for cyber security risks and how the entity's cyber security program is managing these risks.
CISO accountability depends on reliable portfolio information about technology risk, uplift needs, technical debt and critical assets.
Direct - supports CISO accountability for the cyber security program and most critical technology resources.
Portfolio reporting must provide the CISO with current information on cyber risks, control gaps, critical assets, remediation progress and accepted residual risks.
02. Entity Protective Security Roles and Responsibilities
The Accountable Authority approves security governance arrangements that are tailored to the entity's size, complexity and risk environment.
Portfolio governance must operate within approved security governance arrangements and match NDIA's risk environment and complexity.
Direct - applies to NDIA portfolio boards, architecture forums, investment gates and rationalisation decisions.
Technology portfolio governance must align with NDIA security governance, including defined decision rights, risk escalation paths and evidence requirements.
Annual planning, capability alignment and roadmaps
A security plan is developed, implemented and maintained to address the mandatory elements of the plan.
The security plan should be reflected in portfolio roadmaps so funded work addresses mandatory PSPF security actions and controls.
Direct - portfolio planning must incorporate security plan commitments affecting ICT assets.
The annual technology portfolio plan must trace relevant security plan actions to portfolio initiatives, owners, funding decisions and delivery timeframes.
Annual planning, capability alignment and roadmaps
The Accountable Authority approves the entity's security plan.
Accountable Authority approval of the security plan relies on accurate portfolio commitments and resource implications.
Supporting - TPP provides ICT inputs and evidence for approved security planning.
Portfolio owners must provide timely ICT asset, risk, investment and remediation information needed to support security plan approval.
Annual planning, capability alignment and roadmaps
The security plan is considered annually and reviewed at least every two years to confirm its adequacy and ability to adapt to shifts in the entity's risk, threat or operating environment.
Security plan reviews must be synchronised with the portfolio cycle to respond to threat, risk and operating environment changes.
Direct - NDIA technology roadmaps and prioritisation must be reviewed at least annually and when major risk changes occur.
NDIA must review the technology portfolio plan annually and update priorities when security threats, risks, architecture or operating context materially change.
Annual planning, capability alignment and roadmaps
Procedures are developed, implemented and maintained to ensure all elements of the entity's security plan are achieved.
Procedures are needed so portfolio processes reliably deliver security plan outcomes across applications, infrastructure and data assets.
Direct - portfolio procedures should show how PSPF-related actions move through intake, prioritisation and delivery.
Portfolio procedures must define how security plan actions are captured, prioritised, funded, tracked and reported through portfolio governance.
Executive reporting, assurance evidence and monitoring
Develop, establish and implement security monitoring arrangements to identify the effectiveness of the entity's security plan and establish a continuous cycle of improvement.
Continuous improvement requires monitoring of technology control gaps, legacy risk, remediation and portfolio delivery effectiveness.
Direct - monitoring should be embedded in portfolio dashboards and lifecycle reviews.
Portfolio reporting must include security and resilience measures, control uplift progress, technical debt remediation and ageing risk exceptions to support continuous improvement.
Executive reporting, assurance evidence and monitoring
The annual protective security report is provided to the entity's Minister.
Annual protective security reporting needs reliable ICT portfolio evidence for technology risks, assets and remediation progress.
Supporting - NDIA portfolio records should feed entity-level PSPF reporting to ministers and oversight bodies.
Portfolio governance must maintain evidence that supports NDIA annual protective security reporting for ICT assets, risks and uplift activities.
Executive reporting, assurance evidence and monitoring
The annual protective security report is submitted to the Department of Home Affairs.
Home Affairs reporting requires traceable portfolio information on the technology estate and PSPF implementation status.
Supporting - applies to the evidence and data outputs from NDIA ICT portfolio management.
The technology portfolio function must supply complete, current and auditable ICT portfolio information for NDIA PSPF reporting submissions.
Executive reporting, assurance evidence and monitoring
The Accountable Authority approves the entity's annual protective security report and confirms that they have verified the report's content.
Accountable Authority attestation requires validated ICT portfolio data, not unmanaged spreadsheets or unverified estimates.
Supporting - ICT portfolio owners must validate evidence used in entity reporting.
Portfolio evidence used for protective security reporting must be reviewed and validated by accountable technology owners before submission for executive approval.
Executive reporting, assurance evidence and monitoring
Entities cooperate with the Department of Home Affairs' assurance activities to review annual protective security reports.
Assurance activities require defensible records of decisions, risk acceptances, asset status and remediation commitments.
Supporting - NDIA must be able to produce portfolio evidence during Home Affairs assurance activities.
NDIA must retain auditable records of portfolio decisions, asset classifications, risk acceptances, exceptions and remediation actions for assurance purposes.
Executive reporting, assurance evidence and monitoring
The annual Cyber Security Survey is submitted to the Australian Signals Directorate.
Cyber Security Survey responses depend on accurate technology asset, control maturity and uplift information.
Supporting - portfolio data should feed cyber survey inputs led by cyber security functions.
Portfolio records must support collection of cyber security survey data, including asset coverage, control maturity, remediation status and critical dependency information.
Risk appetite, ownership, exceptions and technical debt
The Accountable Authority determines their entity's tolerance for security risks and documents in the security plan.
Portfolio prioritisation needs defined security risk tolerance to decide when to invest, remediate, retire, replace or accept residual risk.
Direct - applies to prioritisation and risk acceptance for NDIA technology assets.
Portfolio decisions must apply NDIA's documented security risk tolerance when prioritising investment, rationalisation, remediation or risk acceptance for ICT assets.
Risk appetite, ownership, exceptions and technical debt
A risk steward (or manager) is identified for each security risk or category of security risk, including shared risks.
Security risks associated with technology assets need named stewards to own treatment and residual risk decisions.
Direct - applies to each material risk linked to applications, infrastructure, data assets and shared services.
Each material ICT portfolio risk must have an assigned risk steward or owner responsible for treatment plans, residual risk advice and status reporting.
Risk appetite, ownership, exceptions and technical debt
The Accountable Authority considers the impact that their security risk management decisions could potentially have on other entities, and shares information on risks where appropriate.
Technology decisions can affect other entities through shared services, integrations, data exchanges and supply chain dependencies.
Direct - applies where NDIA systems, data or services interoperate with other entities.
Portfolio assessments must consider security impacts on connected entities and require risk information sharing where NDIA changes may affect shared government services or data flows.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance

The entity is accountable for the management of security risks arising from procuring goods and services and ensures procurement and contract decisions do not expose the entity or the Australian Government to an unacceptable level of risk.
Procurement and sourcing choices shape NDIA's technology risk, supplier exposure and long-term technical debt.
Direct - applies to all ICT procurement, renewal and sourcing decisions in the portfolio.
ICT procurement and sourcing decisions must include security risk assessment before approval and must not expose NDIA or government to unacceptable residual risk.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance

Procurement, contracts and third-party outsourced arrangements contain proportionate security terms and conditions to ensure service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements.
Security requirements must be built into contracts to ensure portfolio suppliers meet PSPF obligations.
Direct - applies to technology investments involving vendors, managed services, cloud or subcontractors.
Business cases and procurement plans for ICT portfolio items must specify proportionate PSPF security terms, controls, evidence and reporting obligations for suppliers.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance
Entity ensures service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements as detailed by the entity.
Supplier compliance must be managed as part of the portfolio lifecycle, not only during contract award.
Direct - applies to service providers and contractors supporting NDIA ICT assets.
Technology owners must ensure providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with specified PSPF obligations throughout delivery and operation of portfolio assets.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance

Contractual security terms and conditions require service providers to report any actual or suspected security incidents to the entity, and follow reasonable direction from the entity arising from incident investigations.
Supplier incident reporting obligations protect NDIA's ability to respond to cyber and security events affecting portfolio assets.
Direct - applies to outsourced, cloud, software, infrastructure and support arrangements.
ICT supplier contracts must require actual or suspected security incidents to be reported to NDIA and require suppliers to follow reasonable investigation and remediation directions.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance
Government entities providing outsourced services provide IRAP assessment reports to the government entities consuming, or looking to consume, their services.
IRAP evidence is a key input to risk-based decisions when consuming outsourced government services.
Supporting - applies when NDIA consumes government-provided outsourced technology services.
Portfolio assessments for outsourced government technology services must obtain and consider available IRAP assessment reports before selection or continued use.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance

Contract security terms and conditions are monitored and reviewed to ensure the specified security controls, terms and conditions are implemented, operated and maintained by the contracted provider, including any subcontractors, over the life of a contract.
Security terms lose value unless monitored through the contract and asset lifecycle.
Direct - applies to ongoing portfolio assurance for supplier-delivered ICT services.
Portfolio lifecycle reviews must verify that contracted security controls and obligations are implemented, operated and maintained by providers and subcontractors.
Decommissioning, migration, supplier exit and disposal
Contractual terms and conditions include appropriate security arrangements for the completion or termination of the contract.
Exit, completion and termination activities can expose data, credentials, assets and service continuity if not planned early.
Direct - applies to rationalisation, decommissioning, transition and contract exit decisions.
ICT portfolio plans must include secure transition, exit and termination requirements for supplier arrangements, including data return, disposal, access removal and continuity controls.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance
Procurement and contract decisions consider the security risks before engaging providers operating under foreign ownership, control or influence.
Foreign ownership, control or influence can create security and sovereignty risk in technology asset decisions.
Direct - applies to vendor, product, managed service and hosting decisions.
Foreign ownership, control or influence risk
Portfolio sourcing decisions must assess FOCI risk for technology providers, products and services before procurement, renewal or continued use.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance
Security risks arising from contractual arrangements for the provision of goods and services are managed, reassessed and adjusted over the life of a contract.
Contractual security risk changes over time as threats, suppliers, services and subcontractors change.
Direct - applies across the operational lifecycle of supplier-supported technology assets.
Supplier-related security risks must be reassessed during portfolio reviews and contract milestones, with treatment plans adjusted when risk or service conditions change.
Sourcing strategy, contracts, supplier risk and assurance
Secure and verifiable third-party vendors, providers, partners and associated services are used unless business operations require use, and the residual risks are managed and approved by the CISO.
Portfolio decisions should favour secure, verifiable suppliers and require CISO approval for residual risks from exceptions.
Direct - applies to third-party technology vendors, services, platforms and integrations.
NDIA must use secure and verifiable technology vendors and services unless a documented business need exists and residual risk is approved by the CISO.
Risk appetite, ownership, exceptions and technical debt

Where exceptional circumstances prevent or affect an entity's capability to implement a PSPF requirement or standard, the Accountable Authority may vary application, for a limited period of time, consistent with the entity's risk tolerance.
Temporary variation from a PSPF requirement must be controlled so portfolio delivery pressures do not create unmanaged exceptions.
Direct - applies where portfolio items cannot meet mandatory PSPF or security standards on schedule.
Exceptions, waivers and time-bound risk acceptance
Any portfolio exception to a PSPF requirement or standard must be time-limited, justified, risk-assessed and approved consistently with NDIA risk tolerance.
Risk appetite, ownership, exceptions and technical debt
Decisions to vary implementation of a PSPF requirement or standard due to exceptional circumstances are documented in the entity's security plan.
Documented variation decisions are needed for transparency, assurance and alignment with the entity security plan.
Direct - applies to security exceptions arising from portfolio initiatives or legacy assets.
Exceptions, waivers and time-bound risk acceptance
Approved technology portfolio exceptions must be recorded in the portfolio register and provided for inclusion in the entity security plan where required.
Risk appetite, ownership, exceptions and technical debt
Decisions to implement an alternative mitigation measure that meets or exceeds a PSPF requirement or standard are reviewed and reported annually.
Alternative mitigation measures require annual review to confirm they remain equal or stronger than the PSPF requirement.
Direct - applies to compensating controls used for legacy, transitional or constrained ICT assets.
Portfolio owners must document compensating controls, map them to the relevant PSPF requirement and review their effectiveness and continued need at least annually.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
A business continuity plan is developed, implemented and maintained to respond effectively and minimise the impacts of significant business disruptions to the entity's critical services and assets.
Business continuity depends on identifying critical technology services and investing in resilience, recovery and redundancy.
Direct - applies to NDIA critical applications, platforms, infrastructure, data stores and integrations.
Resilience, continuity and critical service dependencies
Technology portfolio planning must identify critical ICT services and assets and prioritise investment needed to meet continuity, recovery and resilience requirements.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
Plans for managing a broad range of emergencies are integrated within the business continuity plan.
Emergency management and continuity planning must be reflected in ICT roadmaps for critical infrastructure and services.
Supporting - applies where ICT assets underpin emergency or continuity response capabilities.
Resilience, continuity and critical service dependencies
Portfolio plans for critical ICT services must align with business continuity and emergency management plans, including recovery, access, communications and dependency requirements.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing

The value, importance or sensitivity of official information is assessed by the originator by considering the potential damage to the government, the national interest, organisations or individuals that would arise if the information's confidentiality were compromised.
Information value and sensitivity determine required controls and should influence investment and rationalisation priorities.
Direct - applies to data assets, information systems and applications processing official information.
Data and application portfolio assessments must classify information by value, importance and sensitivity before investment, design, migration, sharing or disposal decisions.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
The minimum protections and handling requirements are applied to protect OFFICIAL and security classified information.
Minimum protections must be planned and costed so portfolio assets can handle OFFICIAL and classified information appropriately.
Direct - applies to systems storing, processing, communicating or protecting official information.
Portfolio decisions must confirm that applications, infrastructure and data assets can meet minimum protection and handling requirements for their information classification.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
The Australian Government Security Caveat Standard and special handling requirements imposed by the controlling authority are applied to protect security caveated information.
Security caveats impose special handling requirements that affect architecture, access, hosting and lifecycle choices.
Conditional - applies where NDIA handles caveated information in ICT systems or data holdings.
Systems and data assets handling caveated information must be identified in the portfolio and planned with required caveat-specific access, storage and handling controls.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing

The Australian Government Email Protective Marking Standard is applied to protect OFFICIAL and security classified information exchanged by email in and between Australian Government entities, including other authorised parties.
Email and collaboration systems in the portfolio must support required protective marking for information exchange.
Direct - applies to email, messaging, collaboration and workflow platforms used for government information exchange.
Portfolio decisions for email and collaboration capabilities must require support for Australian Government email protective marking obligations.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing

The Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard's 'Security Classification' property (and where relevant, the 'Security Caveat' property) is applied to protectively mark information on technology systems that store, process or communicate security classified information.
Recordkeeping metadata for classification and caveats must be supported by systems that manage official records and information assets.
Direct - applies to records, case management, content, data and knowledge management platforms.
Information metadata and system capability requirements
Systems that store, process or communicate classified information must support required security classification and caveat metadata in records and information holdings.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
Apply the Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard's 'Rights' property where the entity wishes to categorise information content by the type of restrictions on access.
Rights metadata helps enforce access restrictions and should be considered in data and records platform planning.
Direct - applies where NDIA systems categorise information access restrictions.
Information metadata and system capability requirements
Portfolio requirements for records and content platforms must include capability to capture and apply rights metadata where NDIA restricts access by information category.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
Entity implements operational controls for its information holdings that are proportional to their value, importance and sensitivity.
Operational controls should be proportional to information value, importance and sensitivity, which are key portfolio planning inputs.
Direct - applies to all information holdings supported by NDIA applications, infrastructure and data platforms.
Technology portfolio decisions must apply proportional operational controls based on the assessed value, importance and sensitivity of information holdings.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
An auditable register is maintained for TOP SECRET information and accountable material.
Highly sensitive accountable material requires auditable registers and must be recognised in portfolio and data asset governance.
Conditional - applies only if NDIA holds TOP SECRET information or accountable material in ICT-enabled holdings.
Where NDIA holds TOP SECRET information or accountable material, related systems must be identified in the portfolio and linked to auditable accountable material registers.
Decommissioning, migration, supplier exit and disposal

OFFICIAL and security classified information is disposed of securely in accordance with the Minimum Protections and Handling Requirements, ISM, the Records Authorities, a Normal Administrative Practice and the Archives Act 1983.
Rationalisation and decommissioning can create disposal risk unless information disposal requirements are built into lifecycle plans.
Direct - applies to application retirement, data migration, storage decommissioning and archive decisions.
Portfolio rationalisation and decommissioning plans must include secure disposal of official and classified information in accordance with applicable records and security requirements.
Decommissioning, migration, supplier exit and disposal

Security classified information is appropriately destroyed in accordance with the Minimum Protections and Handling Requirements when it has passed the minimum retention requirements or reaches authorised destruction dates.
Classified information destruction must be managed when assets reach authorised destruction dates or decommissioning milestones.
Conditional - applies where NDIA systems or media hold classified information.
Decommissioning plans for systems or media containing classified information must require approved destruction after minimum retention and authorised destruction requirements are met.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing

Access to security classified information or resources is only provided to people outside the entity with the appropriate security clearance (where required) and a need-to-know, and is transferred in accordance with the Minimum Protections and Handling Requirements.
Portfolio-enabled information sharing must enforce clearance, need-to-know and approved transfer controls.
Direct - applies to systems enabling access by external parties to classified information or resources.
Portfolio proposals enabling external access to classified information or resources must require appropriate clearance, need-to-know and secure transfer controls before approval.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
The Memorandum of Understanding between the Commonwealth, States and Territories is applied when sharing information with state and territory government agencies.
Intergovernmental data sharing requires recognised arrangements to be reflected in system and integration planning.
Conditional - applies to NDIA systems sharing information with state or territory agencies.
Technology initiatives that enable sharing with state or territory agencies must identify and apply the relevant Commonwealth, state and territory information-sharing arrangements.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
An agreement or arrangement is in place before security classified information or resources are disclosed or shared with a person or organisation outside of government.
External disclosure of classified information requires formal arrangements and should be a gate for technology enablement.
Conditional - applies when portfolio initiatives share classified information or resources outside government.
Portfolio initiatives must not enable external sharing of classified information or resources unless approved security agreements or arrangements are in place.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
Provisions are met concerning the security of people, information and resources contained in international agreements and arrangements to which Australia is a party.
International agreements may impose security obligations that affect data, hosting, access and supplier choices.
Conditional - applies to ICT capabilities supporting international agreements or arrangements.
Technology portfolio proposals involving international agreements must identify required security provisions and incorporate them into architecture, sourcing and data controls.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing

Australian Government security classified information or resources shared with a foreign entity is protected by an explicit legislative provision, international agreement or international arrangement.
Foreign entity sharing requires explicit legal or international authority and should be assessed before designing or funding capability.
Conditional - applies to systems or data flows involving foreign entities.
Portfolio initiatives must not enable sharing of Australian Government classified information or resources with foreign entities without approved authority and security controls.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing

Australian Government security classified information or resources bearing the AUSTEO caveat is never shared with a person who is not an Australian citizen, even when an international agreement or arrangement is in place, unless an exemption is granted.
AUSTEO caveat restrictions require systems and access models that prevent unauthorised non-citizen access.
Conditional - applies only where NDIA systems handle AUSTEO-caveated information.
Systems handling AUSTEO-caveated information must enforce citizenship and access restrictions and must not enable sharing outside permitted exemptions.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing
Australian Government security classified information or resources bearing the AGAO caveat is not shared with a person who is not an Australian citizen, except as specified.
AGAO caveat restrictions affect user eligibility, sharing functions and information access design.
Conditional - applies only where NDIA systems handle AGAO-caveated information.
Systems handling AGAO-caveated information must enforce required access restrictions and approved sharing rules before operational use.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing

Where an international agreement or arrangement is in place, security classified foreign entity information or resources are safeguarded in accordance with the provisions set out in the agreement or arrangement.
Foreign entity information may require controls defined by international agreements and must be recognised in portfolio planning.
Conditional - applies where NDIA systems hold or process foreign entity classified information.
Portfolio assets handling foreign entity classified information must implement safeguards required by the applicable agreement or arrangement.
Information handling, protected information and data sharing

Australian Government security classified information or resources shared with a foreign non-government stakeholder is protected by an explicit legislative provision, international agreement or international arrangement.
Foreign non-government sharing requires explicit authority and affects integration, access and data protection design.
Conditional - applies to initiatives sharing classified information or resources with foreign non-government stakeholders.
Portfolio initiatives must not share Australian Government classified information or resources with foreign non-government stakeholders without approved authority and controls.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual cyber security principles are applied during all stages of the lifecycle of each system.
The ISM must inform technology lifecycle decisions so security is built into planning, design, operation, change and retirement.
Direct - central to NDIA application, infrastructure and data portfolio lifecycle management.
Secure technology lifecycle and ISM alignment
NDIA must apply ASD ISM cyber security principles throughout the lifecycle of each portfolio technology asset, from concept through retirement.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual controls and cyber security guidelines are applied on a risk-based approach.
Risk-based ISM controls affect cost, feasibility, prioritisation and acceptance of technology investments.
Direct - applies to investment cases, architecture decisions, remediation and rationalisation.
Secure technology lifecycle and ISM alignment
Portfolio investment and change decisions must identify applicable ISM controls, assess implementation risk and include funded treatment or approved risk acceptance.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls

The Authorising Officer authorises each technology system to operate based on the acceptance of the residual security risks associated with its operation before that system processes, stores or communicates government information or data.
Systems must not operate with government information until residual risks are accepted by an Authorising Officer.
Direct - applies to new systems, major upgrades, cloud services and platform changes.
A technology system must not process, store or communicate government information or data until authorised to operate by the relevant Authorising Officer.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
Decisions to authorise (or reauthorise) a new technology system or make changes to an existing technology system are based on the ISM's risk-based approach to cyber security.
Authorisation and reauthorisation are key portfolio gates for new systems and significant change.
Direct - applies to portfolio intake, funding gates, major change and release governance.
New technology systems and significant changes to existing systems must include ISM-based security assessment and authorisation or reauthorisation evidence before operational release.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
The technology system is authorised to the highest security classification of the information and data it will process, store or communicate.
The highest data classification determines hosting, access, control and authorisation requirements for the asset.
Direct - applies to systems processing, storing or communicating NDIA information and data.
Each portfolio technology system must be classified and authorised to the highest security classification of information or data it will process, store or communicate.
Application portfolio management and asset inventory

A register of the entity's authorised technology systems is developed, implemented and maintained, and includes the name and position of the Authorising Officer, system owner, date of authorisation, and any decisions to accept residual security risks.
An authoritative system register is foundational for portfolio planning, risk management, rationalisation and reporting.
Direct - core requirement for NDIA technology portfolio management.
NDIA must maintain an authoritative register of authorised technology systems including system owner, Authorising Officer, authorisation date and accepted residual security risks.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls

Each technology system's suitability to be authorised to operate is reassessed when it undergoes significant functionality or architectural change, or where the system's security environment has changed considerably.
Significant functional, architectural or security environment changes can invalidate prior portfolio risk and authorisation decisions.
Direct - applies to change, upgrade, migration, rationalisation and threat-driven reassessment.
Portfolio governance must require reassessment of a system's suitability to operate after significant functionality, architecture or security environment change.
Standards catalogue, approved technology catalogue and reuse
The TikTok application is prevented from being installed, and existing instances are removed, on government devices, unless a legitimate business reason exists.
Prohibited applications must be excluded from approved technology catalogues and managed as application portfolio risk.
Direct - applies to application portfolio governance and device/software standards.
Approved technology catalogue and prohibited technologies
NDIA's technology catalogue must prevent installation or continued use of prohibited applications on government devices unless an approved exception applies.
Standards catalogue, approved technology catalogue and reuse
The CSO or CISO approves any legitimate business reason for the use of the TikTok application on government devices and ensures specified mitigations are in place.
Exceptions for prohibited technologies require senior security approval and documented mitigations to prevent unmanaged portfolio risk.
Conditional - applies only where a legitimate business reason for a prohibited application is proposed.
Approved technology catalogue and prohibited technologies
Any exception to use a prohibited application must be approved by the CSO or CISO and must include documented mitigations before use.
Risk appetite, ownership, exceptions and technical debt
The Australian Signals Directorate's temporary mitigations for legacy IT are applied to manage legacy information technology that cannot yet be replaced.
Legacy IT is a portfolio and technical debt issue; temporary mitigations must be applied until replacement or remediation.
Direct - applies to legacy applications, unsupported platforms, infrastructure and data technologies.
Legacy technology, technical debt and remediation roadmap
Legacy ICT assets that cannot yet be replaced must have ASD temporary mitigations, a documented risk treatment plan and a funded remediation or retirement roadmap.
Cloud, data centre, gateway, facility and zone assurance
Technology assets and their components, classified as SECRET or below are stored in the appropriate Security Zone based on their aggregated security classification or business impact level.
Physical storage and hosting decisions for technology assets depend on classification and business impact level.
Conditional - applies to technology assets classified SECRET or below or with relevant business impact levels.
Infrastructure placement, hosting and security zones
Portfolio hosting and storage decisions for technology assets must align security zone placement with aggregated classification and business impact level.
Cloud, data centre, gateway, facility and zone assurance
Technology assets and their components classified as TOP SECRET are stored in suitable SCEC-endorsed racks or compartments within an accredited Security Zone Five area.
TOP SECRET assets need specialised approved storage environments that must be planned before investment or operation.
Conditional - applies only where NDIA operates or proposes TOP SECRET technology assets.
Infrastructure placement, hosting and security zones
TOP SECRET technology assets must not be approved for operation unless suitable SCEC-endorsed racks or compartments in accredited Security Zone Five are available.
Cloud, data centre, gateway, facility and zone assurance

Outsourced facilities that house technology assets and their components with a catastrophic business impact level are certified by ASIO T4 physical security and accredited by ASD before they are used operationally.
High-impact outsourced hosting can create unacceptable risk unless facility certification and ASD accreditation are verified.
Conditional - applies to outsourced facilities housing catastrophic business impact technology assets.
Hosting, data centre and facility assurance
Portfolio decisions for outsourced facilities housing catastrophic-impact technology assets must require ASIO T4 certification and ASD accreditation before operational use.
Decommissioning, migration, supplier exit and disposal
Technology assets are disposed of securely in accordance with the Information Security Manual.
Secure disposal is essential to technology rationalisation and prevents residual data, media and hardware risk.
Direct - applies to retirement of devices, infrastructure components, storage, applications and supporting media.
Technology asset retirement and rationalisation plans must include secure disposal or sanitisation in accordance with the ISM and must retain disposal evidence.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls

A cyber security strategy and uplift plan is developed, implemented and maintained to manage the entity's cyber security risks in accordance with the ISM and the Guiding Principles to Embed a Zero Trust Culture.
The cyber security strategy and uplift plan should drive portfolio investment priorities and target-state architecture.
Direct - applies to portfolio prioritisation, roadmap alignment and cyber uplift funding.
Cyber uplift alignment and Zero Trust culture
The ICT portfolio roadmap must align with NDIA's cyber security strategy and uplift plan, including Zero Trust-aligned capabilities and prioritised risk treatments.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
Patch applications mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Application patchability is a key lifecycle criterion for investment, modernisation and rationalisation decisions.
Direct - applies to all managed applications and software components in the portfolio.
Application portfolio decisions must prioritise assets that can meet required application patching maturity and must remediate, replace or retire non-compliant assets.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
Patch operating systems mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Operating system patchability and support status drive infrastructure risk and technical debt priorities.
Direct - applies to servers, endpoints, platforms, appliances and operating system components.
Essential Eight alignment - operating system patching
Infrastructure portfolio decisions must maintain required operating system patching maturity and prioritise remediation or retirement of unsupported or non-compliant platforms.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
Multi-factor authentication mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
MFA capability affects platform selection, identity architecture and prioritisation of legacy remediation.
Direct - applies to applications, platforms, remote access and privileged access paths.
Essential Eight alignment - identity and MFA
Portfolio investments must require multi-factor authentication capability for applicable systems and prioritise remediation where legacy assets cannot meet MFA requirements.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
Restrict administrative privileges mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Restricting administrative privileges requires investment in privileged access controls and influences platform lifecycle decisions.
Direct - applies to systems, infrastructure, SaaS, cloud and administrative tooling.
Essential Eight alignment - privileged access management
Portfolio plans must include privileged access controls for technology assets and prioritise remediation where administrative access cannot be effectively restricted or monitored.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
Application control mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Application control affects endpoint, server and platform standards and must be considered in approved technology decisions.
Direct - applies to managed endpoints, servers and execution environments.
Approved technology standards must support required application control maturity, and portfolio exceptions must be risk-assessed, approved and remediated.
ISM, Essential Eight, authorisation, access and cyber controls
Restrict Microsoft Office macros mitigation strategy is implemented to Maturity Level Two under ASD's Essential Eight Maturity Model.
Macro risk is linked to productivity platforms and legacy processes; remediation can require workflow or application changes.
Direct - applies to Microsoft Office, collaboration, document automation and business applications using macros.
